quests.instruction: Choose the sentence that is a rebuttal (it answers the opposing point directly).
quests.prompt: Objection: Cash-free shops exclude people who do not have bank cards.
options: Shops could keep a small cash option for those customers while moving most payments to cards.
Cards and phones are used for payments in many countries around the world.
Some customers do not enjoy using cards or phones when they pay.
Cash-free shops are becoming more common in the centre of many towns.
quests.hint: A rebuttal offers a solution or a reason that answers the objection.
quests.explanation: Keeping a cash option answers the exclusion problem. The alternatives give background or repeat the objection.

quests.instruction: Choose the best rebuttal.
quests.prompt: Objection: Flexible deadlines may encourage students to delay their work.
options: Deadlines are set by teachers at the start of each term for every class.
Some students prefer to hand in work early rather than close to a deadline.
Students in other schools follow different deadline policies from ours.
A short extension request form makes students plan ahead, so deadlines still matter.
quests.hint: The reply must deal with the risk of delay.
quests.explanation: A request form keeps students accountable, answering the concern about delay. The alternatives don't address the risk.

quests.instruction: Which sentence is NOT a rebuttal to the objection?
quests.prompt: Claim: Cyclists should be required by law to wear helmets. Objection: A law might discourage people from cycling.
options: Cyclists should wear helmets because helmets make riding safer.
Helmets can be lent free at cycle hire points, so cost need not stop anyone.
Public campaigns could explain why helmets matter before any penalties begin.
A phased law could start with young riders, where the safety benefit is greatest.
quests.hint: Three sentences deal with the fear of fewer cyclists. One just repeats the claim.
quests.explanation: The first sentence restates the claim without answering the objection. The others all offer ways to keep people cycling.

quests.instruction: Choose the strongest rebuttal.
quests.prompt: Claim: Students should sometimes mark each other's work. Objection: Students may be unfair or careless when marking.
options: Marking is an important skill in a number of different jobs.
Clear mark schemes and teacher spot-checks would keep the marking consistent and fair.
Teachers also make mistakes when they mark large piles of work.
Students are usually friendly with each other in most classes.
quests.hint: The strongest reply answers the exact worry about unfair marking.
quests.explanation: Mark schemes and spot-checks reduce unfairness. The other choices add friendly feelings, criticise teachers or mention job skills.

quests.instruction: Choose the strongest rebuttal.
quests.prompt: Claim: Cities should plant more street trees. Objection: Tree roots can damage pavements and cost money to repair.
options: Trees have been planted in cities for many hundreds of years.
Trees make streets look prettier in every season of the year.
Choosing species with shallow roots and leaving enough soil space reduces the damage.
Repairs to pavements can be expensive for the council to organise.
quests.hint: Which reply deals with the damage itself?
quests.explanation: The correct reply gives a way to prevent the damage. The other choices give unrelated benefits or repeat the concern.

quests.instruction: Choose the strongest rebuttal.
quests.prompt: Claim: Job adverts should show salary ranges. Objection: It might cause resentment among existing staff.
options: Resentment is a feeling that can affect the mood of a team, and it often grows when people hear things second-hand.
Job adverts are read by many people who are looking for work, and they often decide within seconds whether to apply.
Reviewing current pay against the ranges would let companies fix unfair gaps before publishing.
Some staff already know roughly what their colleagues are paid, because pay is often discussed in the canteen.
quests.hint: Reply to the cause of the resentment.
quests.explanation: Fixing unfair gaps removes the reason for resentment. The rest are facts or descriptions.

quests.instruction: Which reply MISSES the point of the objection?
quests.prompt: Objection: Self-checkout machines put cashiers out of work.
options: Some shops have used the change to move staff into new roles.
Staff hours can be shifted to help customers on the shop floor.
Shops can retrain cashiers to manage stock or assist shoppers.
Self-checkouts are faster for customers buying only a few items.
quests.hint: Which reply talks about something other than jobs?
quests.explanation: Speed for customers doesn't answer the concern about jobs. The rest deal with what happens to the staff.

quests.instruction: Which reply does NOT answer the objection?
quests.prompt: Objection: A shorter working week may reduce customer service hours.
options: Opening hours can stay the same if teams work staggered days.
Rotating staff so the shop stays open five days keeps service hours the same.
Online support could cover the extra day when the office is closed.
Employees generally enjoy having a longer weekend to rest.
quests.hint: The objection is about service hours, not about staff enjoyment.
quests.explanation: Enjoying a longer weekend doesn't address service hours. The other replies suggest ways to keep service available.

quests.instruction: Which reply actually answers the objection?
quests.prompt: Objection: Homework apps make students spend more time on screens.
options: Homework has been set in schools for centuries in many countries, and it has taken many different forms over time.
Apps can replace worksheets, so screen time shifts rather than grows, and teachers can set time limits.
Some apps have colourful characters and small rewards for progress, which many younger students find motivating.
Apps are very popular among students of many different ages, and new homework apps appear every year.
quests.hint: The reply must deal with the amount of screen time.
quests.explanation: Replacing worksheets and setting limits speaks to the screen-time concern. The alternatives are unrelated facts.

quests.instruction: Which sentence misrepresents the opposing view (a strawman)?
quests.prompt: Opposing view: Some parents want limits on how long children play video games at night.
options: So these parents want to ban all games and never let children have fun.
These parents want fixed limits on evening playing time.
They worry that late gaming leaves children tired at school.
They are asking for agreed limits, not a total ban.
quests.hint: A strawman exaggerates the other side's view to make it easy to reject.
quests.explanation: The first sentence turns 'limits' into 'ban all games'. The remaining options describe the parents' position accurately.

quests.instruction: Which response treats the opposing view fairly?
quests.prompt: Opposing view: Many residents worry that more evening events will increase noise.
options: Residents seem to think nobody should ever leave their houses after dark, and they want the town to close early.
Their worry about noise is reasonable, so events could end at ten and use sound limits.
They apparently hate any kind of fun or community life, and would like the events to be stopped altogether.
These residents simply want the town to be boring and empty, and they resent anyone who enjoys a busy evening.
quests.hint: Fair responses describe the concern as it was stated.
quests.explanation: The right response accepts the noise concern and offers a fix. The others distort the residents' view into extremes.

quests.instruction: Which reply commits a strawman?
quests.prompt: A colleague suggests keeping routine meetings under 30 minutes.
options: What would we do when a decision needs longer discussion?
So you want us to stop talking to each other at work altogether.
Perhaps we could set a 30-minute limit for routine updates only.
I see the point of shorter meetings, but some topics need more time.
quests.hint: Compare the reply with what the colleague actually said.
quests.explanation: The colleague asked for shorter routine meetings, not no talking at all. The other replies respond to the real suggestion.

quests.instruction: Which reply disagrees respectfully?
quests.prompt: A commenter writes: 'Open offices are bad for concentration.'
options: Nobody serious would believe that argument for a moment.
That is a ridiculous thing to say and it is completely wrong.
I see why you say that, but my experience in an open office was different.
You clearly have never worked in an office, or you would know better.
quests.hint: Respectful disagreement acknowledges the other view without attacking the person.
quests.explanation: This reply accepts the view might make sense and explains a different experience. The others insult the commenter.

quests.instruction: Choose the sentence that disagrees politely.
quests.prompt: You are replying to a colleague's email about the cost of a training course.
options: Cost is not important, and I will not discuss it any further.
Anyone can see that your concerns about the cost are exaggerated.
I take your point about the cost, though I wonder whether the training would pay for itself.
Your point about cost is silly, and the training is obviously worth it.
quests.hint: Look for wording that engages with the point.
quests.explanation: 'I take your point' acknowledges the concern and 'I wonder' invites discussion. The others dismiss or insult.

quests.instruction: Which reply challenges the idea, not the person?
quests.prompt: Alex suggests: 'We should stop offering discounts.'
options: Only someone who never shops would suggest an idea like that.
Discounts bring in new customers, so removing them could reduce sales.
Alex should stay out of pricing decisions from now on.
Alex has never really understood how customers think or behave.
quests.hint: Which reply talks about discounts rather than Alex?
quests.explanation: The correct reply gives a reason about the effect of removing discounts. The remaining options criticise Alex personally.

quests.instruction: Choose the claim that acknowledges exceptions accurately.
quests.prompt: Topic: workplace training.
options: All workplace training should be short, so that nobody is taken away from their tasks for long.
In most workplaces, short training sessions work better than full-day courses, except for complex technical skills.
Full-day courses are useful only for new staff, because experienced staff already know most of the material.
Training sessions are held in many workplaces around the country, usually at the start of a new financial year.
quests.hint: An accurate claim admits where it does not apply.
quests.explanation: This claim includes 'most' and an exception. The alternatives overgeneralise or only describe.

quests.instruction: Which sentence acknowledges an exception without weakening the claim?
quests.prompt: Claim: Students should read for pleasure every day.
options: Reading takes place in schools, homes and public libraries, and many students also read on the bus.
Busy students can skip reading when exams are near, since reading for pleasure is not that important.
Every student should read for pleasure every day, whatever their circumstances, so that the habit stays strong.
Daily reading suits most students, though those with heavy exam schedules may need a shorter routine.
quests.hint: Notice how the exception is named and the main claim remains.
quests.explanation: The best sentence keeps the claim for most students and adapts for a group. The alternatives overstate, retreat or describe.

quests.instruction: Choose the phrase that makes the claim accurate and limited.
quests.prompt: '____, public transport costs less than owning a car.'
options: For the whole of history
In most cities
At every possible moment
In absolutely every situation
quests.hint: The best phrase does not promise more than the writer can support.
quests.explanation: 'In most cities' limits the claim to what is reasonable. The other choices promise too much.

quests.instruction: Put the sentences in order: claim, objection, reply, conclusion.
quests.prompt: Arrange the sentences about online sign-ups.
options: A phone number and a drop-in desk could serve those who cannot use the website.
Community events should use online sign-up sheets.
Critics say older residents may struggle to use them.
With that backup, online sign-ups would save organisers time without excluding anyone.
quests.hint: The reply must follow the objection it answers.
quests.explanation: The claim leads, the objection follows, the reply solves it, and the conclusion brings the argument together.

quests.instruction: Order the sentences.
quests.prompt: Arrange the sentences about paid time for volunteering at work.
options: Companies should offer paid time for volunteering.
Limiting it to two days a year and planning around busy periods keeps work on track.
The company would gain motivated staff while the community gains helpers.
Some managers fear that projects will be delayed by absences.
quests.hint: Look for the sentence that solves the manager's fear.
quests.explanation: The claim opens, the fear is stated, the plan answers it, and the closing sums up the benefits.

quests.instruction: Order the sentences.
quests.prompt: Arrange the sentences about learning to cook.
options: Small, regular practice would prepare them well for living independently.
Even one simple recipe a week builds basic skills, so short sessions are enough.
Young people should learn to cook before leaving home.
Some say busy families have no time to teach them.
quests.hint: The objection is about time, so the reply should be about a short amount of time.
quests.explanation: The claim opens, the objection about time follows, the reply shows little time is needed, and the closing looks ahead.

quests.instruction: Choose the revision that best strengthens the weak rebuttal.
quests.prompt: Objection: Free entry to the sports hall for students would cost too much. Weak rebuttal: 'It won't really cost that much.'
options: The cost is not something that should worry anyone at all, since the council has plenty of money in reserve.
It will cost very little, and nobody should complain about it, because students deserve free access anyway.
The hall is empty most weekday afternoons, so extra visitors would add almost no running cost.
Sports halls are a public service, so cost is not a real issue, and the council should simply pay for it.
quests.hint: A stronger rebuttal gives a reason or evidence for its claim.
quests.explanation: The empty afternoons explain why the cost is low. The other choices repeat the weak claim with stronger words.

quests.instruction: Choose the best way to strengthen the rebuttal.
quests.prompt: Objection: Working from home makes teams less creative. Weak rebuttal: 'That is not true.'
options: That is definitely not true, whatever anyone says about it, and nobody should waste time on the question.
Teams can hold regular video workshops and in-person days, which keep ideas flowing.
Creative people are creative anywhere they choose to work, so the place of work makes no difference.
Some teams are more creative than other teams are, whether they work at home or in an office.
quests.hint: Replace a denial with a way of solving the problem.
quests.explanation: This answer explains how creativity can be maintained. The rest deny, assert or state the obvious.

quests.instruction: Which rebuttal is the strongest because it includes specific evidence?
quests.prompt: Objection: Recycling bins in flats attract pests.
options: Pests can be a problem in many kinds of building and location, and flats are no different from houses.
Nobody has ever proved that recycling bins cause pests to appear, so the complaint should be ignored.
Recycling bins are found in most blocks of flats across the country, and most residents use them each week.
In the block that switched to sealed lids and weekly cleaning, pest complaints fell to zero within two months.
quests.hint: Look for a real result linked to a solution.
quests.explanation: The block's result shows the problem can be fixed. The alternatives give general facts or a weak 'nobody has proved' argument.

quests.instruction: Choose the paragraph with a claim, an opposing view, a concession and a fitting reply.
quests.prompt: Four paragraphs argue for a quiet room at school.
options: Schools should provide a quiet room for students who feel overwhelmed. Some teachers worry that students may use it to avoid lessons. That risk is real, but many schools have rooms of different sizes. Students would then return to class calmer and ready to learn.

Schools should provide a quiet room for students who feel overwhelmed. Some teachers just want students to suffer in silence. A booking system with time limits would keep the room for genuine need. Students would then return to class calmer and ready to learn.

Schools should provide a quiet room for students who feel overwhelmed. A booking system with time limits would keep the room for genuine need. Students would then return to class calmer and ready to learn. Teachers are busy people.

Schools should provide a quiet room for students who feel overwhelmed. Some teachers worry that students may use it to avoid lessons. That risk is real, but a booking system with time limits would keep the room for genuine need. Students would then return to class calmer and ready to learn.
quests.hint: Check that the reply answers the worry that was mentioned.
quests.explanation: The correct paragraph names a fair worry, concedes it and answers it. The alternatives give an irrelevant reply, distort the teachers' view or never mention an objection.

quests.instruction: Choose the best paragraph.
quests.prompt: Four paragraphs argue that companies should pay for staff training.
options: Companies should pay for staff training courses. Some employers fear that trained staff will leave for better jobs. That can happen, but staff who feel valued tend to stay longer, and a training agreement can protect the investment. Better skills also help the whole company.

Companies should pay for staff training courses. Some employers fear that trained staff will leave for better jobs. That can happen, but training courses are offered in many towns. Better skills also help the whole company.
Companies should pay for staff training courses. Employers who disagree clearly do not care about their workers. Staff who feel valued tend to stay longer. Better skills also help the whole company.

Some employers fear that trained staff will leave for better jobs. That can happen, but staff who feel valued tend to stay longer. A training agreement can protect the investment. Better skills also help the whole company.
quests.hint: A strong paragraph states its claim first and replies to the specific worry.
quests.explanation: The right paragraph states a claim, concedes a real worry and answers it with two reasons. The remaining options give a weak reply, use a strawman or omit the claim.

quests.instruction: Choose the paragraph that treats the opposing view most fairly.
quests.prompt: Four paragraphs argue that restaurants should offer smaller portions at lower prices.
options: Restaurants should offer smaller portions at lower prices. Some owners say that smaller plates make customers feel they are getting less. Customers feel very hungry after any portion. Diners would waste less food and spend less.

Restaurants should offer smaller portions at lower prices. Some owners say that smaller plates make customers feel they are getting less. That concern is understandable, but clear menus and fair prices can show the value. Diners would waste less food and spend less.

Restaurants should offer smaller portions at lower prices. Some owners say that smaller plates make customers feel they are getting less. Owners only care about profit, so their concern can be ignored. Diners would waste less food and spend less.

Restaurants should offer smaller portions at lower prices. Owners think customers want huge plates and nothing else. Clear menus and fair prices can show the value. Diners would waste less food and spend less.
quests.hint: Look for the paragraph that states the other side accurately before replying.
quests.explanation: The correct paragraph describes the owners' concern accurately and replies to it. The others dismiss motives, give an unrelated reply or exaggerate the owners' view.

quests.instruction: Which sentence is the rebuttal?
quests.prompt: 'Parks should stay open after dark for evening walkers. Safety in dark places may be a concern. That is a fair worry. Better lighting and a few patrols would make evening visits safer than the empty streets nearby.'
options: Parks should stay open after dark for evening walkers.
Safety in dark places may be a concern.
That is a fair worry.
Better lighting and a few patrols would make evening visits safer than the empty streets nearby.
quests.hint: The rebuttal answers the objection with a solution or reason.
quests.explanation: The last sentence responds to the safety worry with specific measures. The rest give the claim, the objection and the concession.

quests.instruction: Select the TWO sentences that show respectful disagreement.
quests.prompt: A student is replying to a classmate who wants laptops allowed in lectures.
options: Anyone who defends laptops in lectures is obviously not paying attention.
That idea is nonsense, and I refuse to consider it any further.
You make a fair point about note-taking, though I wonder whether the distraction outweighs it.
I understand that laptops help some students take notes, but they can also tempt others to browse.
quests.hint: Look for replies that acknowledge the other student's point.
quests.explanation: The correct replies recognise a valid point before disagreeing. The alternatives insult or dismiss.

quests.instruction: Choose the best answer to the objection.
quests.prompt: Claim: Neighbourhoods should set up swap shops. Objection: People might leave broken items.
options: Swap shops are popular in several countries and cities, and many of them are run entirely by local volunteers.
Some people do leave broken items there, which is unfortunate, but it is part of running a swap shop.
Broken items can be thrown in the bin once they are found, so the shop does not need any rules for donations.
A volunteer check at drop-off and a clear list of accepted items would keep quality high.
quests.hint: The reply should reduce the problem before it happens.
quests.explanation: The best answer offers a practical way to prevent broken items. The remaining options accept the problem, add background or suggest a late fix.
